en: Udāna 5.3 Suppabuddhakuṭṭhisutta Thus have I heard—
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time there was a leper in Rājagaha named Suppabuddha—
a poor man, a wretched man, a miserable man.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was seated, surrounded by a large assembly, teaching the Dhamma.
Suppabuddha the leper saw that great multitude gathered from afar.
Having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
“Without a doubt, some kind of solid food or soft food must be being distributed here.
What if I were to go over to where that great crowd of people is?
Perhaps I might obtain some solid food or soft food there.”
Then Suppabuddha the leper approached that large crowd of people.
Suppabuddha the leper saw the Blessed One sitting, surrounded by a great assembly, teaching the Dhamma.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
“Nothing at all, whether hard food or soft food, is being distributed here.
This ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma to the assembly.
What if I were also to listen to the Dhamma?”
He sat down right there to one side,
thinking, "I too shall hear the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One, with his own mind, encompassed the minds of the entire assembly.
“Who here is capable of understanding the Dhamma?
Then the Blessed One saw Suppabuddha the leper sitting in that assembly.
Having seen him, this thought occurred to him:
“Indeed, this one here is capable of understanding the Dhamma.
Addressing the leper Suppabuddha, he gave a graduated discourse, namely:
a talk on generosity, a talk on virtuous conduct, and a talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that Suppabuddha the leper had a ready mind, a pliant mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, he then set forth that Dhamma exposition which is uniquely realized by Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take the dye;
In this very way, as Suppabuddha the leper sat on that very seat, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arose:
"Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.
Then Suppabuddha the leper had seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged into the Dharma.
Having crossed over doubt and being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence and no longer depending on others in the Teacher’s dispensation,
Suppabuddha the leper rose from his seat, approached the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One,
sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Suppabuddha the leper said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—[so it has been done by the Blessed One].”
"In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
Then Suppabuddha the leper, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma,
rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had said. Rising from his seat, he paid homage to the Blessed One,
circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then, not long after Suppabuddha the leper had departed, a cow with a young calf rushed at him and took his life.
Thereupon, a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, that leper named Suppabuddha, who was instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, has passed away.
What is his destination? What is his future state?
“Bhikkhus, the leper Suppabuddha was wise; he practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and did not trouble me with legal matters concerning the Dhamma.”
“Bhikkhus, with the complete destruction of three fetters, Suppabuddha the leper is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu addressed the Blessed One:
“What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason why Suppabuddha the leper became thus?”
“A poor man among men, a wretched man among men, a miserable man among men?
“Once upon a time, monks, Suppabuddha the leper was the son of a banker in this very city of Rājagaha.
While going out to a park, he saw the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī entering the city for alms.”
Seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
"Where is this leper wandering about with his leper's garment?
Having spat and passed him by on the left, he departed.
As the result of that karma, he was cooked in hell for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years.
By the remaining residue of that very same karma, he became a leper in this very city of Rājagaha—a poor man, a wretched man, a miserable man.
Having approached the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, he undertook faith, he undertook virtue, he undertook learning, he undertook generosity, and he undertook wisdom.
Thus, having relied upon the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, and having undertaken faith, undertaken virtue, undertaken learning,
undertaken generosity, and undertaken wisdom, with the breakup of the body, after death,
he was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Thus, there he outshines the other devas both in beauty and in glory.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“Like one with eyes avoiding uneven ground...”
While there is still effort possible,
a wise person in this world of living beings should avoid evil deeds.
The third.
